learn.title: 1 — Taylor and Scientific Management
learn.body:
Frederick Winslow Taylor was a mechanical engineer who believed that industrial inefficiency could be cured by treating the factory as a scientific problem. His method: time and study every worker motion with a stopwatch, identify the "one best way" to perform each task, then enforce that method on workers.

Scientific management radically separated thinking from doing. Workers would no longer decide how to do their jobs — that was management's responsibility. Workers would simply execute the prescribed motions. Taylor argued this was good for everyone (higher wages from higher productivity) but it stripped workers of craft knowledge and autonomy.

learn.title: 2 — Ford and the Moving Assembly Line
learn.body:
Henry Ford took Taylor's ideas further. In 1913, Ford installed the moving assembly line at Highland Park, Michigan — the most radical reorganization of production in industrial history. Instead of workers carrying parts to a chassis, the chassis moved past stationary workers, each performing one or two repetitive motions endlessly.

The result was dramatic: the time to build a Model T dropped from 12.5 hours to 93 minutes. Prices fell, sales skyrocketed. But the human cost was enormous: the work was physically numbing, required no skill, and the turnover rate was extreme — Ford had to hire 963 workers for every 100 he wanted to keep.

learn.title: 3 — The $5 Day and Social Control
learn.body:
Ford's response to turnover was the famous $5/day wage in January 1914 — roughly double the prevailing rate. This looked like generosity; in reality, it was social engineering. Workers who received the $5 rate had to pass inspection by Ford's Sociological Department: they had to live "correctly" — no drinking, debt, or "improper" domestic arrangements.

Ford's reading of the relationship between employers and workers was explicitly paternalistic and anti-union. His chapter "The Terror of the Machine" argues that machines are not threatening — it is mismanagement and greed that create labor conflict. This is a deeply ideological document that students should read critically.

learn.title: 4 — Hughes: Engineers and the 'Labor Problem'
learn.body:
Thomas P. Hughes situates Taylor and Ford within the broader history of American technological enthusiasm. Hughes's concept of the "labor problem" — how to control and motivate an industrial workforce — explains why scientific management and Fordism were so appealing to engineers and industrialists.

For Hughes, Taylorism and Fordism were not just technical innovations — they were systems of power that embedded management control into the physical structure of the workplace. The assembly line, by its design, prevented workers from having any discretion or craft knowledge. The engineered workplace became a mechanism of social control.

anki.a: Taylor's method: systematically time and study every worker motion, identify the 'one best way,' and enforce it — separating thinking (management) from doing (workers).

anki.q: What was Ford's key innovation with the moving assembly line (1913)?
anki.a: Instead of workers moving to parts, parts moved past stationary workers on a moving line — reducing Model T production from 12.5 hours to 93 minutes.
Mechanical engineer and management theorist; father of 'scientific management'; developed time-and-motion studies to optimize factory productivity.

anki.q: What was Ford's $5/day wage and what was its real purpose?
anki.a: Announced January 1914, it doubled prevailing wages. Real purpose: reduce extreme turnover caused by the numbing assembly line work. Workers also had to pass the Ford Sociological Department's inspection of their private lives.

anki.q: What is the 'labor problem' as Hughes uses the term?
anki.a: The central challenge of industrial capitalism: how to control, discipline, and motivate workers who would otherwise resist the demands of repetitive, deskilled industrial production.

anki.q: What did scientific management strip from workers?
anki.a: Craft knowledge and autonomy — workers no longer decided how to do their jobs; that became management's exclusive domain.

anki.q: Who was Thomas P. Hughes and what is American Genesis about?
anki.a: Leading historian of technology; American Genesis (1989) traces American technological enthusiasm 1870–1970, including the rise of Taylorism and Fordism.
The combination of mass production (assembly line), high wages, and mass consumption — Ford's insight that workers must be paid enough to buy the products they make.

anki.q: What was the Ford Sociological Department?
anki.a: Ford's inspection program that determined who received the $5/day wage — workers had to demonstrate proper private life: no drinking, no debt, "correct" domestic arrangements.

anki.q: How does Ford's 'The Terror of the Machine' chapter argue about labor conflict?
anki.a: Machines themselves are not the problem — mismanagement and greed cause labor conflict. Ford presents a self-serving, paternalistic view of worker-employer relations that students should read critically.

anki.q: Why was turnover so extreme at Ford's Highland Park plant?
anki.a: The assembly line work was physically numbing and required no skill or craft — workers found the conditions intolerable; Ford had to hire 963 workers for every 100 retained.

anki.q: How did Taylorism and Fordism function as systems of power, per Hughes?
anki.a: They embedded management control into the physical structure of the workplace — the assembly line design prevented worker discretion, making social control a technological feature.

anki.q: What is the significance of separating 'thinking' from 'doing' in Taylor's system?
anki.a: It transferred all knowledge and decision-making to management, deskilling workers and making them easier to control and replace — a fundamental shift in the balance of power.

anki.q: How did Ford's assembly line change car prices?
anki.a: Dramatically reduced production costs allowed Ford to cut Model T prices repeatedly — making the automobile accessible to the middle class for the first time.

anki.q: What critique would Donna Riley (Week 1) make of Taylor's and Ford's approach to engineering?
anki.a: Taylor and Ford are prime examples of engineers who solved assigned problems (efficiency, productivity) without asking who benefits and who is harmed — classic uncritical problem-solving.

anki.q: Why is Ford's chapter 'The Terror of the Machine' called ideological?
anki.a: Ford presents a one-sided account that blames labor conflict on greed and mismanagement rather than on the dehumanizing conditions his own system created — it should be read critically as a primary source.

options: Using computers to schedule factory production
Applying science to optimize product design
Systematically studying worker motions to enforce the 'one best way' — separating thinking (management) from doing (workers)
A union strategy for fair wages
quiz.explanation: Taylor's system used time-and-motion studies to identify optimal work methods, then forced workers to follow them — stripping craft knowledge from workers and giving management total control.

quiz.q: What was Ford's key innovation with the assembly line (1913)?
options: Robots performing all assembly tasks
Workers moving to different stations throughout the day
Parts moving past stationary workers, each doing one repetitive task
A slower, more careful production method
quiz.explanation: The moving assembly line had parts flow past stationary workers — reducing Model T production time from 12.5 hours to 93 minutes.

quiz.q: What was the REAL purpose of Ford's $5/day wage?
options: Pure generosity toward the working class
Compliance with new federal labor laws
Reducing extreme turnover caused by the numbing, deskilled assembly line work
To outcompete other automakers' wages
quiz.explanation: Ford had to hire ~963 workers for every 100 he wanted to keep — the $5 wage (with surveillance strings attached) was an engineering solution to the human cost of the assembly line.

quiz.q: What does Thomas Hughes mean by the 'labor problem'?
options: The technical challenge of designing ergonomic workplaces
How to control, discipline, and motivate workers who resist industrial production
The shortage of skilled workers in early 20th-century America
Legal disputes between engineers and their employers
quiz.explanation: Hughes frames Taylorism and Fordism as solutions to the central challenge of industrial capitalism: engineering systems that controlled workers structurally, not just through supervision.

quiz.q: What did Taylorism strip from workers?
options: Their wages
Craft knowledge and job autonomy — decisions about how to work became management's exclusive domain
Physical access to the factory floor
The ability to form unions
quiz.explanation: By defining 'the one best way' and enforcing it, Taylor's system deskilled workers and transferred all knowledge and decision-making to management.
